description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of 2 Kings (wave A, the Elijah cycle: chapters 1, 2). v1.0.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, claude-opus-5-5) creates the overlay. It holds nine conventions shared verbatim with the 1-kings-woh overlay (Hebrew proper-name transliteration, the elohim referent/article rule, the 'man of the Elohim' title, the nefesh scope and spelling, the ruach transliteration, Ketiv/Qere, the MT baseline at versional cruxes and versification, 'YHWH of hosts', and Ba'al) and four 2 Kings-specific decisions (Ba'al-Zevuv of Eqron, the sons of the prophets, the double portion of 2:9, and the chariot and horses of fire of 2:11-12). Shared entries carry identical text and appliesTo in both overlays; extend both together.

entries.source: אֵלִיָּהוּ / אֵלִיָּה ; אַחְאָב ; אִיזֶבֶל ; אֲחַזְיָהוּ / אֲחַזְיָה ...
entries.translit: ʾēliyyāhû / ʾēliyyâ ; ʾaḥʾāḇ ; ʾîzeḇel ; ʾăḥazyāhû / ʾăḥazyâ ...
entries.lemma: Hebrew personal names and toponyms of the Elijah-Elisha narratives (1 Kgs 17 - 2 Kgs 2 and following)
entries.partOfSpeech: proper nouns (personal names, divine names of foreign deities, toponyms) - book-wide rendering convention
entries.literal: the Hebrew name forms as written in the Masoretic Text
entries.standardEnglish: the conventional English (KJV/ASV) forms: Elijah, Ahab, Jezebel, Obadiah, Carmel, Baal, Jezreel, Samaria, Jordan, Israel ...
entries.wohChoice: WoH transliteration of the Hebrew name (Eliyahu, Ach'av, Izevel, Ovadyahu, Karmel, Ba'al, Yizre'el, Shomron, Yarden, Yisra'el ...), normalized to the long theophoric form where the MT alternates (ʾēliyyâ / ʾēliyyāhû -> Eliyahu; ʾăḥazyâ / ʾăḥazyāhû -> Achazyahu); a small set of names fixed in English usage is kept in English (Moab, Aram, Damascus, Horeb, Gilgal). Equivalence table: Eliyahu = Elijah; Elisha = Elisha; Ach'av = Ahab; Achazyahu = Ahaziah; Izevel = Jezebel; Ovadyahu = Obadiah; Chaza'el = Hazael; Yehu = Jehu; Nimshi = Nimshi; Shafat = Shaphat; Yehoram = Jehoram; Yehoshafat = Jehoshaphat; Ba'al = Baal; Ba'al-Zevuv = Baal-zebub; Karmel = Carmel; Kerit = Cherith; Qishon = Kishon; Shomron = Samaria; Tzarfat = Zarephath; Tzidon = Sidon; Gil'ad = Gilead; Yarden = Jordan; Yizre'el = Jezreel; Avel-Mecholah = Abel-meholah; Eqron = Ekron; Yericho = Jericho; Beit-El = Bethel; Be'er Sheva = Beersheba; Yisra'el = Israel; Yehudah = Judah; Avraham = Abraham; Yitzchaq = Isaac; Ya'aqov = Jacob. Kept in their familiar English form: Moab, Aram, Damascus, Horeb, Gilgal, Asherah, and the gentilic 'Tishbite'.
entries.rationale: Kings continues the narrative Hebrew of Genesis and Exodus, and the Wheel of Heaven Translation renders the Torah narrative books with transliterated name forms (genesis-woh: Avraham, Ya'aqov, Yosef, Beit-El, Be'er Sheva; exodus-woh: Yisra'el, Aharon, Ya'aqov), so the Kings narratives adopt the same practice rather than switching to the KJV forms used in the Latter-Prophets volumes (isaiah-woh, ezekiel-woh). The transliteration makes the theophoric element visible on the surface: Eliyahu ('my El is Yah'), Ovadyahu ('servant of Yah'), Achazyahu ('Yah has grasped') and Yehoram/Yehoshafat carry the Yahwistic name that the Elijah cycle sets against Ba'al, and the cycle's central confession at 1 Kgs 18:39 (YHWH hûʾ hāʾĕlōhîm) is a play on the prophet's own name (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10, 2001; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL). The MT writes the short forms ʾēliyyâ (2 Kgs 1:3, 4, 8, 12) and ʾăḥazyâ (2 Kgs 1:2) beside the long forms; both are standard variants of the same name (the short -yâ form predominates in post-exilic books), the ASV and all major versions normalize them, and the translation does likewise, recording the MT spelling in commentary. The Exodus exception ('Moses', 'Pharaoh') is a grandfathered single-book decision for two names whose English form is a household word; it is not extended here, because a mixed surface ('Elijah ... Ach'av ... Izevel') is less consistent than either pure option. This is a presentation convention with no interpretive content: every name is given with its conventional English equivalent in the table above and in the commentary at first occurrence in each chapter, so a reader can match the translation to the ASV and to the English editions of the Raëlian books, which quote these chapters as 'Elijah' and 'Elisha'. Founder preference point: the alternative (KJV forms throughout) is a mechanical substitution using the equivalence table and would require no other change. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01, zarazinsfuss): Hebrew transliterated long forms with tz for tsade are kept book-wide, and each chapter title adds the English form of its principal name in parentheses, e.g. 'Eliyahu (Elijah)', for findability.

entries.source: הָאֱלֹהִים / אֱלֹהִים / אֱלֹהֵיכֶם / אֱלֹהֵי עֶקְרוֹן / כֹּה־יַעֲשׂוּן אֱלֹהִים
entries.translit: hāʾĕlōhîm / ʾĕlōhîm / ʾĕlōhêḵem / ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn / kōh-yaʿăśûn ʾĕlōhîm
entries.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine plural; Kings application of the central elohim-as-translation convention
entries.literal: the god(s) / god(s) / your god(s) / the god(s) of Ekron / so may god(s) do
entries.standardEnglish: God (of YHWH); god / gods (of Baal, of Baal-zebub, in Jezebel's oath) - ASV
entries.wohChoice: (1) YHWH referent with the Hebrew article (hāʾĕlōhîm): 'the Elohim' (1 Kgs 18:21, 24, 37, 39; 19:8). (2) YHWH referent, anarthrous predicate or genitive: 'Elohim' without article ('that you are Elohim in Yisra'el', 18:36; 'no Elohim in Yisra'el', 2 Kgs 1:3, 6, 16; 'fire of Elohim', 2 Kgs 1:12). (3) Construct with a possessor: 'YHWH your/my Elohim', 'the Elohim of Yisra'el'. (4) Non-YHWH referent (Ba'al, Ba'al-Zevuv, the deities of Izevel's oath): lower-case 'elohim', number following the Hebrew agreement ('your elohim', 'he is an elohim', 'the elohim of Eqron', 'So may the elohim do' with the plural verbs yaʿăśûn / yôsipûn).
entries.rationale: The central elohim-as-translation entry fixes the untranslated plural 'Elohim' and the narrative article; it was written for Genesis 1, where every occurrence refers to the one deity, and it does not say how to render the same lexeme when the Hebrew applies it to another god. Carmel (1 Kgs 18) is built on exactly that contrast: Eliyahu tells the Ba'al prophets to call on 'the name of your ʾĕlōhîm' (18:24, 25) and mocks Ba'al with kî-ʾĕlōhîm hûʾ 'for he is a god' (18:27), and the people's verdict is YHWH hûʾ hāʾĕlōhîm 'YHWH, he is the Elohim' (18:39); 2 Kgs 1 sets ʾĕlōhîm bəyiśrāʾēl against Ba'al-Zevuv ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn. Using one written form for both sides would erase the contrast the narrative depends on, and translating only the non-YHWH cases as 'god' would break the corpus decision to leave the lexeme untranslated, so the case distinction (capital for YHWH, lower case otherwise) follows the precedent of exodus-woh at Ex 20:3 ('other elohim', central elohim-aherim-other-gods-monolatry-vs-monotheism-scholarly-dispute-cross-corpus). The article follows the Hebrew where the Hebrew is anarthrous in predicate or genitive position (18:36 kî-ʾattâ ʾĕlōhîm; 2 Kgs 1:12 ʾēš-ʾĕlōhîm), because adding 'the' there would turn a classifying predicate ('that you are God in Israel', BDB ʾĕlōhîm 3) into an identification the Hebrew does not make; the narrative-subject article rule of the central entry is unaffected. Agreement also follows the Hebrew: Izevel's oath at 19:2 governs ʾĕlōhîm with plural verbs (as Ben-Hadad's oath does at 1 Kgs 20:10), unlike the same oath formula in Israelite mouths with singular verbs (1 Kgs 2:23; 1 Sam 3:17; 14:44; 2 Sam 3:9), so it is rendered as a plural 'the elohim'; the ASV's supplied 'to me' is not in the Hebrew of 19:2 and is not added. The capital/lower-case distinction is an editorial device, since Hebrew script has no case; the commentary states this at the first relevant verse.

entries.partOfSpeech: construct noun phrase used as a prophetic title
entries.literal: man of the God / a man of God
entries.standardEnglish: man of God (ASV, KJV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'man of the Elohim' where the Hebrew has the article (1 Kgs 17:18; 2 Kgs 1:9, 11, 12, 13); 'a man of Elohim' where it does not (1 Kgs 17:24; 2 Kgs 1:10)
entries.rationale: ʾîš (hā)ʾĕlōhîm is the title Kings gives to Eliyahu, Elisha and the anonymous Judahite prophet of 1 Kgs 13; it designates a person who belongs to and acts for the deity, and it is used more in Kings than in any other book (BDB ʾîš 5; Cogan, 1 Kings, on 13:1). The central elohim-as-translation convention requires 'Elohim' to remain untranslated, so 'man of God' cannot be used without breaking the corpus decision; the remaining question is the article, and the Hebrew itself alternates. In 2 Kgs 1:9-13 the alternation carries meaning: the first two captains address Eliyahu with the articular title ʾîš hāʾĕlōhîm, Eliyahu answers the first with the anarthrous ʾim-ʾîš ʾĕlōhîm ʾānî 'if I am a man of God' (1:10), the second time with the articular form (1:12), and the narrator then calls the fire ʾēš-ʾĕlōhîm (1:12); the ʾîš / ʾēš wordplay ('man' / 'fire') is widely noted (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11, 1988). Following the Hebrew article keeps that alternation visible, which a uniform 'man of God' or 'man of Elohim' would hide. The woman's confession at 1 Kgs 17:24 (ʾîš ʾĕlōhîm ʾattâ), quoted in the English edition of the Raëlian canon as 'a man of God', is anarthrous and is rendered 'a man of Elohim'; the commentary gives the conventional English.

entries.lemma: nepeš 'throat, breath, life, living being, self'
entries.wohChoice: 'nefesh' (transliterated, house spelling) only where the nepeš is named as the life-component that departs or returns (1 Kgs 17:21-22, governed by central tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula); idiomatic English elsewhere: 'life' (19:2, 3, 4b, 10, 14; 2 Kgs 1:13-14), reflexive 'himself' (19:4a), and 'as you yourself live' for the oath ḥê-napšəḵā (2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6)
entries.rationale: nepeš has a wide range (throat, breath, appetite, life, living being, the person him- or herself; HALOT nepeš 1-9; Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 1974), and the central glossary already rejects the Platonic 'soul' for it (nefesh-chayah) and transliterates it where it names the life that leaves the body at death (tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula, which cites 1 Kgs 17:21-22 as the return-of-nepeš counterpart to Gen 35:18). In 1 Kgs 17:21-22 the nepeš of the boy 'returns into his inward part' (tāšāḇ ... ʿal-qirbô), so the noun names exactly that life-component and is transliterated; at every other site in the wave the word is part of an idiom ('to seek someone's nepeš' = to seek to kill; 'to go for one's nepeš' = to flee for one's life; wayyišʾal ʾeṯ-napšô lāmûṯ 'he asked for himself that he might die'; ḥê-napšəḵā 'by your life'), where English 'life' or a reflexive renders the idiom accurately and a transliteration would suggest a technical sense that is not there. The oath ḥay-YHWH wəḥê-napšəḵā (2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6; also 1 Sam 1:26; 20:3; 25:26; 2 Kgs 4:30) swears by YHWH's life and the addressee's life; 'as you yourself live' (cf. NJPS 'as you live') keeps the second oath-member without the ASV's 'soul', in line with nefesh-chayah. Spelling: the central glossary uses 'nefesh' in nefesh-chayah, nefesh-blessing-transfer, karet-penalty-cut-off-from-people and shivim-nefesh, and 'nephesh' only in tzet-nephesh; 'nefesh' (f for the spirantized p, as in Yosef, Shafat, Yehoshafat) is the house spelling, and a central diff proposes normalizing tzet-nephesh's wohChoice accordingly.

entries.source: רוּחַ יְהוָה / רוּחַ אֵלִיָּהוּ / רוּחַ גְּדוֹלָה
entries.translit: rûaḥ YHWH / rûaḥ ʾēliyyāhû / rûaḥ gədôlâ
entries.literal: the wind/breath/spirit of YHWH; the spirit of Elijah; a great wind
entries.standardEnglish: the Spirit of Jehovah (1 Kgs 18:12; 2 Kgs 2:16 ASV); thy spirit / the spirit of Elijah (2 Kgs 2:9, 15); a great and strong wind (1 Kgs 19:11)
entries.wohChoice: 'the ruach of YHWH' where rûaḥ YHWH is an agent that carries the prophet off (1 Kgs 18:12; 2 Kgs 2:16), and 'ruach' for the prophet's rûaḥ that passes from Eliyahu to Elisha (2 Kgs 2:9, 15), so the same Hebrew word stays visible across 2 Kgs 2:9-16; 'wind' where the context is plainly meteorological (rûaḥ gədôlâ wəḥāzāq, 1 Kgs 19:11 three times)
entries.rationale: rûaḥ covers 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit' (BDB; HALOT rûaḥ 1-11), and in the two Elijah passages where rûaḥ YHWH is said to carry a prophet away (1 Kgs 18:12, 'the rûaḥ YHWH will carry you I know not where'; 2 Kgs 2:16, 'lest the rûaḥ YHWH has taken him up and cast him on one of the mountains') commentators divide between a divine 'spirit' and a 'wind of YHWH' (cf. Isa 40:7; Hos 13:15, where rûaḥ YHWH is a wind; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL; Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11). The ASV capital 'Spirit' settles the ambiguity in favour of the later doctrinal concept of a personal Holy Spirit, which the Hebrew does not specify; the corpus precedent for a rûaḥ that physically transports a prophet is ezekiel-woh, which renders rûaḥ YHWH 'the ruach of YHWH' at Ezek 37:1 (cf. central ruach-chayyot, also inferred), and the Kings wave follows it. In 2 Kgs 2 the narrative links the rûaḥ that Elisha asks for (2:9) and that the prophets see resting on him (2:15) with the rûaḥ YHWH they fear has carried Eliyahu off (2:16), right after an ascent in a storm (2:11); a single transliterated term keeps that verbal link visible, which 'spirit' / 'Spirit' / 'wind' in three different places would break. Where the Hebrew is unambiguously meteorological (the wind that tears the mountains at Horeb, 1 Kgs 19:11) the word is translated 'wind', consistent with the central ruach-gedolah-midbar treatment. The entry is inferred, not direct: transliteration is a decision to leave a recognized ambiguity unresolved, and the 'wind' reading of rûaḥ YHWH at 18:12 and 2:16 is defensible but a minority view; the commentary sets out both readings and does not choose between them.

entries.lemma: Ketiv ('what is written', the consonantal text) and Qere ('what is read', the Masoretic reading tradition)
entries.literal: the written consonants vs the vocalized reading
entries.standardEnglish: ASV and all major English versions translate the Qere silently
entries.wohChoice: translate the Qere; record the Ketiv in commentary at every site. Wave A sites: 1 Kgs 17:14 (K tittēn / Q tēt), 17:15 (K 'he and she' / Q 'she and he'), 18:36 (K 'your words' / Q 'your word'), 18:42 (K defective / Q birkāyw 'his knees'), 19:4 (K fem. ʾaḥat / Q masc. ʾeḥād), 2 Kgs 2:16 (K / Q 'the valleys', orthographic)
entries.rationale: The Leningrad Codex marks each Ketiv/Qere pair with the Qere vocalization placed on the Ketiv consonants (or in the margin), and the Masoretic tradition reads the Qere; English Bible translation, including the ASV baseline, follows the Qere in all but a handful of cases (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012, on Ketiv/Qere). None of the six wave-A pairs changes the sense materially: two are grammatical (17:14 finite verb vs infinitive construct; 19:4 gender agreement with rōṯem, which is masculine in 19:5), two are number variants (18:36 'words'/'word'; 18:42 defective spelling of 'his knees'), one is word order (17:15) and one orthographic (2 Kgs 2:16). Translating the Qere keeps the English aligned with the reading tradition and with every major version, while recording the Ketiv in the commentary keeps the consonantal text auditable. The same rule is the project baseline in genesis-woh and exodus-woh; this entry makes it explicit for Kings so later waves can extend the appliesTo list.

entries.source: מִתֹּשָׁבֵי גִלְעָד ; חֲמִשִּׁים אִישׁ ; וַיַּרְא ; שְׁלִשִׁים ; אַף־הוּא ...
entries.translit: mittōšāḇê gilʿāḏ ; ḥămiššîm ʾîš ; wayyarʾ ; šəlišîm ; ʾap̄-hûʾ ...
entries.lemma: Masoretic vocalization and division where the ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate) or modern emendations read otherwise
entries.literal: the MT as vocalized and divided
entries.standardEnglish: ASV follows the MT at these sites; NRSV and some modern versions adopt the versional reading at 1 Kgs 17:1 and 19:3
entries.wohChoice: translate the MT vocalization and verse division; give the versional reading in commentary. Sites: 1 Kgs 17:1 'of the settlers of Gil'ad' (MT mittōšāḇê; LXX ek Thesbōn 'from Tishbe'); 18:4 'fifty men to a cave' (MT singular ḥămiššîm ʾîš; LXX/Peshitta distributive as in 18:13); 18:26 impersonal 'which was given them ... which had been made' (MT singular active verbs); 19:3 'And he saw' (MT wayyarʾ; LXX/Peshitta/Vulgate 'he was afraid', wayyîrāʾ); 2 Kgs 1:13 'the captain of a third fifty' (MT plural šəlišîm); 2 Kgs 2:14 ʾap̄-hûʾ opening the second half, as the major disjunctive on ʾēliyyāhû divides the verse (so also ASV; LXX aphphō is the alternative). Versification: 1 Kgs 18:33-34 follows the MT division (MT 18:34 = ASV 18:33b-34).
entries.rationale: The Wheel of Heaven Translation translates the Masoretic Text and records ancient-version and conjectural readings in the apparatus rather than adopting them in the line; this is the baseline of genesis-woh (e.g., yov-yashuv at Gen 46:13) and exodus-woh (kes-yah-vs-nes-yah at Ex 17:16). At each wave-A site the MT gives a construable sense: 'of the settlers of Gil'ad' is grammatical, if repetitive after 'the Tishbite' (Burney, Notes on the Hebrew Text of the Books of Kings, 1903); wayyarʾ 'he saw' makes sense as 'he saw (how things stood)', even though most moderns prefer the versional 'he was afraid' (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10); the singular verbs at 18:26 can be impersonal; šəlišîm at 2 Kgs 1:13 can be read as 'a third (set)' (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11). Because the MT can be construed at each site, emending it would be a textual-critical decision beyond the remit of a translation that commits to the MT; the alternatives are given in commentary so the reader can see where the major versions differ. Verse numbers follow the Hebrew (the chapter files are keyed to MT refIds); at 1 Kgs 18:33-34 the English versions divide the verses one clause earlier, and the commentary records the difference so that canon or ASV citations by verse number can be matched.

entries.literal: YHWH of armies/hosts; YHWH, God of armies/hosts
entries.standardEnglish: Jehovah of hosts; Jehovah, the God of hosts (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'YHWH of hosts' (1 Kgs 18:15); 'YHWH, the Elohim of hosts' (1 Kgs 19:10, 14)
entries.rationale: The title is rendered as in the isaiah-woh overlay entry yhwh-tzevaot-hosts-isaiah ('YHWH of hosts'), keeping the corpus divine-name style 'YHWH' and the ASV noun 'hosts', so the title reads the same in Kings and in Isaiah. The construction YHWH ṣəḇāʾôṯ (a proper name in apparent construct) is grammatically debated, and the referent of the 'hosts' (Israel's armies, the heavenly host, the divine assembly) is disputed (Mettinger, The Dethronement of Sabaoth, 1982; Cross, Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic, 1973); 'hosts' is the conventional English that leaves both senses open, where 'armies' would narrow it. The expanded form at 19:10, 14 (YHWH ʾĕlōhê ṣəḇāʾôṯ) contains ʾĕlōhîm in construct with a possessor and is rendered by the elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings rule ('the Elohim of hosts'). No transliteration 'Tseva'ot' is introduced, so as not to set the Kings volumes apart from the existing Isaiah rendering.

entries.lemma: baʿal 'owner, lord, husband'; as a divine name, the West-Semitic storm god Baal
entries.partOfSpeech: divine name (normally with the article in Hebrew prose); plural for local manifestations or images
entries.wohChoice: 'Ba'al' without the English article (1 Kgs 18:19, 21, 22, 25, 26, 40; 19:18); plural 'the Ba'als' (18:18); compound divine names hyphenated and transliterated ('Ba'al-Zevuv', 2 Kgs 1)
entries.rationale: Hebrew prose regularly writes the god's name with the article (habbaʿal), a remnant of its origin as the title 'the Lord'; English treats the word as a proper name, and the ASV, NRSV and NJPS all omit the article, so the translation does likewise and records the Hebrew article here and in commentary. The spelling Ba'al with the apostrophe for ʿayin follows the genesis-woh transliteration practice (cf. Ba'al-Chanan, Gen 36:38) and the hebrew-proper-name-transliteration-convention-kings entry. The Ugaritic deity is governed by the central baal-ugaritic-baalu-storm-god-cross-corpus-hebrew-bible-polemic entry, whose wohChoice ('Baʿlu') is limited to Ugaritic sources; this entry is its Hebrew-Bible counterpart and records that the Carmel narrative (rain withheld and restored, fire from the sky) is widely read as a polemic against Baal's storm-god attributes (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10; Smith, The Early History of God, 2nd ed., 2002). The plural habbəʿālîm (18:18) denotes local Baal cults or images and is rendered 'the Ba'als' (ASV 'the Baalim').

entries.lemma: baʿal 'lord' + zəḇûḇ 'fly'; divine name of the deity of Ekron
entries.partOfSpeech: divine name in apposition with a construct title
entries.literal: Lord of the fly / flies, the god of Ekron
entries.wohChoice: 'Ba'al-Zevuv, the elohim of Eqron' (MT form transliterated; lower-case elohim per elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings)
entries.rationale: The MT name baʿal zəḇûḇ means 'Lord of the fly/flies' (LXX Baal muian theon 'Baal-fly god'); many scholars hold that it deforms an original baʿal zəḇûl 'Baal the Prince', since zbl bʿl 'Prince Baal' is a standard Ugaritic epithet and the New Testament has Beelzeboul (Mark 3:22) (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11, 1988; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 2000). Others take 'Lord of flies' as a genuine cult title of a healing or oracular god (cf. Greek Zeus Apomyios), so the deformation hypothesis is likely but not certain. The translation keeps the MT form, which is the text being translated and which the narrative repeats four times (1:2, 3, 6, 16), and puts the reconstruction in commentary, following mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-and-versification-kings. The construct title ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn takes lower-case 'elohim' because the referent is not YHWH, which keeps the contrast with the refrain 'is there no Elohim in Yisra'el?' (1:3, 6, 16).

entries.lemma: bēn 'son'; in construct with a group noun, 'member of'
entries.standardEnglish: the sons of the prophets (ASV, KJV, NJPS 'disciples of the prophets' in some places); company of prophets (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'the sons of the prophets' (ASV preserved; the membership sense explained in commentary)
entries.rationale: bēn in construct with a group noun commonly means 'member of' rather than 'descendant of' (bənê-yiśrāʾēl, bən-ʾāḏām; GKC §128v; BDB bēn 7), so bənê-hannəḇîʾîm are members of a prophetic group, not children of prophets. The term is almost confined to the Elisha narratives (1 Kgs 20:35; 2 Kgs 2:3-15; 4:1, 38; 5:22; 6:1; 9:1), where the groups live together, eat together and address Elisha as 'master' (Wilson, Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel, 1980). 'Company/guild of prophets' (NRSV) states the sense but loses the Hebrew idiom; keeping the ASV form and explaining it in commentary leaves the idiom visible and is consistent with the corpus's 'children of Yisra'el' for bənê yiśrāʾēl.

entries.lemma: peh 'mouth; portion, share' in construct with šənayim 'two'
entries.standardEnglish: a double portion (ASV, KJV, NJPS); a double share (NRSV)
entries.rationale: pî-šənayim is the legal term for the firstborn's inheritance in Deut 21:17, where the firstborn receives 'a share of two' of the father's property, i.e., twice what each other son receives; Elisha asks to be Eliyahu's principal heir, not to have twice Eliyahu's power (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL). The same phrase means 'two-thirds' in Zech 13:8, and some interpreters have read it so here, but the inheritance context (Elisha calls Eliyahu 'my father' in 2:12) favours the Deuteronomy sense. 'A double portion' is the conventional English and is accurate for the inheritance sense; the alternatives are noted in commentary. The object of the inheritance is rûaḥ, governed by ruach-yhwh-and-prophetic-ruach-transliteration-kings.

entries.source: רֶכֶב־אֵשׁ וְסוּסֵי אֵשׁ ; רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו
entries.translit: rekeḇ-ʾēš wəsûsê ʾēš ; rekeḇ yiśrāʾēl ûp̄ārāšāyw
entries.lemma: rekeḇ 'chariot; chariotry (collective)'; sûs 'horse'; ʾēš 'fire'; pārāš 'horseman' or 'horse'
entries.literal: chariot(ry) of fire and horses of fire; the chariot(ry) of Israel and its horsemen
entries.standardEnglish: there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire (ASV, with 'there appeared' supplied); the chariots of Israel and the horsemen thereof (ASV 2:12)
entries.wohChoice: 'a chariot of fire and horses of fire' (2:11, literal construct chains, nothing supplied); 'the chariots of Yisra'el and its horsemen' (2:12, ASV)
entries.rationale: The Hebrew of 2:11 is a verbless presentative clause (wəhinnēh rekeḇ-ʾēš wəsûsê ʾēš) followed by a plural verb (wayyaprîḏû bên šənêhem 'and they separated the two of them'); the translation keeps the construct chains and the plural verb and does not supply the ASV's 'there appeared', which is not in the Hebrew. rekeḇ is the same singular form in 2:11 and 2:12; it can be a single chariot or collective 'chariotry', and the ASV's 'a chariot' / 'the chariots' reflects that range; the translation keeps the ASV and notes in commentary that the lexeme is identical, since Elisha's cry 'the chariots of Yisra'el and its horsemen' is a fixed epithet (repeated for Elisha himself at 2 Kgs 13:14) describing the prophet as Israel's real military strength (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11; von Rad, Old Testament Theology II). pārāšîm can mean 'horsemen' or 'horses/steeds' (HALOT pārāš); the ASV 'horsemen' is kept. The fire-chariot and horses recur at 2 Kgs 6:17 as the heavenly army around Elisha, and divine chariots belong to the wider storm-theophany imagery (Ps 68:18; 104:3; Hab 3:8). The verse is the central Kings citation of the Raëlian canon (The Book Which Tells the Truth, ch. 3), which reads it as the departure of a flying craft; that reading is recorded only as a labelled reception note in the commentary, and the line itself renders the Hebrew literally without technical vocabulary.
